items.title: The gallery guide
items.caption: The museum's fold-out guide, read across a glass table before we split up. This single sheet is the map for everything that follows: six permanent galleries stacked across four levels.
items.text: Gallery Guide. Level 3 — Art Gallery: provides a rotating display of the Central Bank of Malaysia's art collection. Numismatics Gallery: discover the early history of money and go back to a time when a variety of different objects were accepted as currency. Temporary Gallery: the venue for temporary exhibitions — for the latest shows and updates, please visit www.museum.bnm.gov.my. Bank Negara Malaysia Gallery: learn about the important roles and responsibilities of the Central Bank of Malaysia in maintaining the financial and economic health of the country. Economics Gallery: discover how economic policies affect the development of a nation and explore Malaysia's economic progress from independence to the present day. Islamic Finance Gallery: explore early Islamic concepts of commerce and finance, which began in the Middle East and extended to Europe and now influence the entire world. Children's Gallery (Ground floor): filled with hands-on games and activities based on the concept of 'Save, Spend and Share'. Experience the RM1 Million Tunnel with its variety of Malaysian banknote denominations and series. Dedicated to providing visitors with a meaningful engagement with the public: BNM MAG elevates visitor experience through innovative temporary exhibitions, special programmes and outreach activities that strengthen and enrich the community from all walks of life. To discover more, please visit www.museum.bnm.gov.my or follow Facebook @BNM.MAG, Instagram @bnmmag and Twitter @bnm_mag.

items.title: The kijang crest
items.caption: Etched on a glass door: the barking deer, the sun and the crescent moon. The whole institution compressed into one mark.

items.title: “Apa itu Fintech?”
items.caption: A wall of floating coloured cubes introduces fintech in Malay and English — the museum's way of saying that financial technology is not new, just newly named.
items.text: Apa itu Fintech? / What is Fintech? Fintech merupakan aplikasi teknologi dalam kewangan. Fintech is the application of technology in finance. Fintech is any new technological innovation that competes with or precedes traditional financial methods, particularly the delivery of financial services. At its core, Fintech is utilised to help companies, business owners and consumers to better manage their financial operations, processes, and lives by utilising specialised software and algorithms that are used on computers, and increasingly, smartphones. Although it is a relatively new term, technological innovation in finance has been evident since the late 1800s in one form or another. Banks, organisations, and governments are continually trying to improve financial technology and improve services for their customers and citizens.

items.title: Malaysia in the Global Economy
items.caption: A gold globe wrapped in arrows. The claim on the wall is startling when you read it twice: Malaysian trade is worth more than the whole Malaysian economy.
items.text: Malaysia in the Global Economy. Trade has always been a major part of the Malaysian economy. Malaysia's exports have gradually shifted from comprising mainly natural resources in the early days to manufactured goods since the 1980s. Currently, Malaysia is a significant trading nation, with trade accounting for over 100% of GDP and with extensive linkages with over 180 countries in the world.

items.title: International Trade, and the MV Economy
items.caption: A mock container ship — the MV Economy — sits behind the panel. Visitors open labelled containers to see what Malaysia actually ships to each partner.
items.text: Perdagangan Antarabangsa / International Trade. Malaysia's activity in international trade extends to almost every country on the planet. We export and import innumerable products, from raw materials to finished goods. Open the specified containers to know what we trade with our major partners around the world.

items.title: The questions everybody actually asks
items.caption: Instead of a definitions panel, the Economics Gallery opens with the questions people mutter in real life — in Malay, English and Manglish. “Why does my RM100 feel small now?”
items.text: Kenapa harga barang kadang-kadang NAIK? · Cukup tak gaji RM2,700 hidup di KL? · Tahu tak apa itu kadar celik kewangan? · Saya masih tidak bekerja — Apa kesannya pada NEGARA? · What is GDP? · Should I save or spend my money? · I trust e-Payment more now for my daily transactions · Kualiti hidup saya sekarang makin selesa, LAH! · Oh-oh! Are we in crisis? · OPR keeps changing. Can't they be static? · Why does my RM100 feel small now? · Taraf Kehidupan

items.title: Progress of a Nation
items.caption: Five decades, five newspaper front pages, five telephone handsets. Pick one up and the era talks back to you.
items.text: Kemajuan Sebuah Negara / Progress of a Nation. Since independence, the Malaysian economy has successfully developed from a low income to an upper middle-income economy. Malaysia's economic development is a story of well-planned economic strategies and clear long-term visions, while learning from past challenges. MILENIUM BARU 2000-an · ERA PERMODENAN 1990-an · ERA PERINDUSTRIAN 1980-an · ERA PERPADUAN 1970-an · ERA PEMBANGUNAN 1960-an

items.title: Commodities
items.caption: The pre-independence economy on one bright grid: coal, gold, tin, rubber, oil. The panel that lands hardest is the red one — smuggled rubber seeds that changed the course of history.
items.text: Apakah komoditi utama Malaysia sebelum Merdeka? / What were Malaysia's main commodities prior to Independence? Get to know about Malaysia's Commodities. Coal played a major role in fuelling Malaya's economy. Gold has been mined in Malaysia since centuries. Industrial Revolution sparks demand. Smuggled seeds change the course of history — by 1921, Malaya was producing half of the world's total rubber supply. Tin mining began in the early 1820's. Oil drilling began at the Grand Old Lady.

items.title: Five little doors
items.caption: Hinged panels asking economics in the language of a Friday night: the price of water at a stadium, bubble tea going from RM7 to RM9, why RM100 buys less USD some days than others.
items.text: Imagine you are at a stadium to watch a football match. Many people are thirsty and want water, but there are only a few stalls selling mineral water. What do you think will happen to the price of mineral water at the stadium? · Every day, our country is busy! Some people are working, some are shopping for groceries, shops are bustling with business, and our country is actively trading with other countries. When we add up the value of all these activities in a year… what do we call it? · Every day countries like China and United States buy Malaysian products (such as palm oil, electronic goods, etc.) — what is the effect on our economy? · Last year your favourite drink was RM7. Now it's RM9. What does that tell you about prices? · Ever changed money before going on a holiday abroad? Some days, RM100 gives you more USD or IDR, and other days, less. So, what makes the value of ringgit change?

items.title: “Segalanya Bermula Di Sini” — it all begins here
items.caption: Natural rubber, tin ore and oil & gas, presented as the three resources that made the Straits of Malacca worth fighting over.
items.text: Segalanya Bermula Di Sini / The Beginning — Rumusan Sumber Asli / Resource Based. Getah Asli / Natural Rubber. Bijih Timah / Tin Ore. Minyak & Gas / Oil & Gas — Bintang Seterusnya / The Next Star. For many decades, Malaysia was one of the largest producers of natural rubber in the world. More recently, the sector has diversified the sector into the manufacturing industry, which has enhanced the economic value of the commodity to the country. Today, Malaysia is the largest supplier of rubber gloves in the world.

items.title: Biodiesel and the golden crop
items.caption: An oil-palm trunk grows straight out of the gallery floor. Beside it, a fruit bunch under glass and the case for palm-derived biodiesel.
items.text: Biodiesel — Kunci kepada Dunia yang Lebih Hijau / The Key to a Greener World. Biodiesel is a renewable, efficient, environmentally friendly and clean burning alternative fuel that can be used in place of petroleum-based diesel. This type of fuel is derived from renewable natural resources such as vegetable oils and animal fats. The growing importance of biodiesel is beneficial for Malaysia, as palm oil is an important component in producing this fuel. Minyak Sawit / Oil Palm — Tanaman Emas / Golden Crop. It was only in the 1960s that the oil palm industry experienced rapid expansion as it was encouraged by the Malaysian Government, which recognised its potential as a complementary crop to rubber. Needless to say, the palm oil industry quickly became one of the major resource-based industries in the country.

items.title: Oil & Gas, Petrochemicals
items.caption: The Grand Old Lady in a bottle. Malaysia's first oil well managed 83 barrels a day in 1910; by 1929 it reached 15,000.
items.text: Minyak & Gas / Oil & Gas — Bintang Seterusnya / The Next Star. The very first oil well (known as The Grand Old Lady) was drilled by Shell. From 83 barrels per day in its early days, the oil well reached a maximum production of 15,000 barrels per day in 1929. There were no other drilling activities elsewhere in Borneo or Peninsular Malaya until the 1950s. PETRONAS (Petroliam Nasional Berhad) — Incorporated on 17 August 1974, vested with the entire ownership and control of the petroleum resources in Malaysia, and entrusted with the responsibility of developing and adding value to these resources. Petrokimia / Petrochemicals — Daripada Pengimport Kepada Pengeksport / From Importer to Exporter. Petrochemicals are chemical products derived from petroleum and natural gas. They are an important component in the production of a wide range of end products such as plastics, paints and cosmetic pharmaceuticals. Mikroskop / Microscope.

items.title: How the country was wired
items.caption: Power, rail, road and air — the four infrastructures that turned a set of mining towns into an economy. A pair of kerosene lamps sits behind glass for the years before electricity.
items.text: Penjanaan Kuasa / Power Generation — Tiada lagi kegelapan! / No more darkness! Electricity first made its appearance in Malaysia at the turn of the 20th century. The earliest record of power generation can be traced back to a small mining town in Rawang, Selangor. Lampu Minyak Tanah / Kerosene Lamp — The early years of light after fireflies. In Malaysia, most homes used kerosene lamps before electricity was introduced in the 1920s. The word 'kerosene' comes from the Greek 'kerosalanan' which means wax oil. Pengangkutan Rel / Rail Transport — Steaming ahead. In Malaysia, the first railway line was constructed between Taiping and Port Weld in 1885 during the British colonial era. Its purpose was to speed up transportation of tin mining areas to ports along the coast. Pengangkutan Darat / Road Transport — Bridging the gap. Driving on the left side of the road (right-hand drive) has been compulsory since the introduction of motor vehicles in the Federated Malay States in 1903 during British colonial era. The first tolled highway was the 20km Tanjung Malim–Slim River tolled road which was opened to traffic on 16 March 1966. Buses and lorries were charged RM2, while cars and motorcycles were charged RM5 and 50 sen respectively. Pengangkutan Udara / Air Transport — Off to a flying start. Malaysian Airline System (MAS), the country's national airline, was founded in 1947. The first Malayan Airways flight departed Singapore's Kallang Airport and was bound for Kuala Lumpur's Sungai Besi Airport with only five passengers on 2 April 1947.

items.title: “Bagaimana kita melangkah…” — how we progressed
items.caption: The pivot panel of the whole gallery: from commodities to services, electronics and semiconductors. A Panasonic Blu-ray player sits on a shelf as a historical artefact, which is its own kind of humbling.
items.text: Tenaga Penggerak / The Moving Force — Industri / Industrial. The industrial sector is an equally important element of Malaysia's economy. The largest contributors from this sector are the electronics, construction and automotive industries. After the Asian Financial Crisis of the late 1990s, Malaysia experienced an economic boom and underwent rapid development driven partly by advances in the industrial sector. Bagaimana kita melangkah… / How we progressed… The Malaysian economy has undergone a dramatic transformation from its dependence on agriculture and commodity exports, to a more diversified and open economy with strong links to global value chains. Sektor Perkhidmatan / Services Sector — Pemandu Utama / The Key Driver. As Malaysia moves towards becoming a developed nation, greater emphasis has been placed on the development of the services sector to serve as the growth engine to propel and sustain the economy.

items.title: “Bagaimana kita bermula…” — how we started
items.caption: Communication and the mobile phone, next to a fire hydrant in a blue arch. Malaysia's first telephone line was strung in 1874; its first cellular phone was the ATUR 450 in 1985.
items.text: Bagaimana kita bermula… / How we started… Meningkatkan kualiti hidup melalui infrastruktur mampan di Malaysia / Improving quality of life through sustainable infrastructure in Malaysia. Komunikasi / Communication — Bringing the world closer together. Malaysia's first telephone (or telegraph) line was installed in 1874, linking the British Colonial government's Resident's Office in Perak with one of its administrative offices, covering a distance of 45km. Telefon Mudah Alih / Mobile Phone — All at your fingertips. The first cellular phone used in Malaysia was the ATUR 450 by Telekom Malaysia in 1985. Pili bomba pertama dicipta pada tahun 1801 / The first hydrant was invented in 1801. Before the invention of fire hydrants, most places used the bucket method: people would form a line, passing buckets along it and continue until the flames were quenched. Now with fire hydrants, firefighters can just connect a fire hose to the hydrants before releasing the valve to get water.

items.title: The infrastructure wall
items.caption: The full sweep of it — power, rail, road, air, communications — read as one continuous argument about what a state has to build before markets can work.

items.title: Semiconductors: the unsung heroes
items.caption: Penang's 1970s bet, told plainly. Free-trade zones, Clarion and National Semiconductor, and half a century later semiconductors are one of Malaysia's biggest exports.
items.text: Semikonduktor / Semiconductors — Hero Teknologi yang Tidak Didendang / The Unsung Heroes of Technology. The Penang State Government launched Penang Electronics in the 1970s to symbolically promote the manufacturing of semiconductor materials, attracting firms such as Clarion (Japan), followed by National Semiconductor (USA). These firms were able to take advantage of the tax-free export-processing zones, and in turn create employment opportunities. Today, semiconductor materials are one of Malaysia's major exports. The material forms the basic blocks of modern electronics. Virtually every device around us uses semiconductors including mobile phones, computers, digital cameras, and video game consoles. Jurutera Elektronik / Electronics Engineer.

items.title: Down the chip tunnel
items.caption: A circuit board at the end of a gold-lit tunnel, the photographer reflected back at himself in the lens at the far end.

items.title: An Atmel chip, enshrined
items.caption: A ceramic Atmel package on a plinth, lit like a relic. Which, in a gallery about how Malaysia earns its living, it more or less is.
items.text: ATMEL AT9…

items.title: Consumer Electronics: the game changer
items.caption: 1965, when Japanese investors entered the local market and started making electronics for Malaysian consumers — the beginning of a sector that still carries the country's exports.
items.text: Elektronik Pengguna / Consumer Electronics — Titik Perubahan / The Game Changer. The consumer electronics industry began in 1965 when Japanese investors entered the local market, manufacturing electronic products for Malaysian consumers. This major sub-sector of the electrical and electronic industry is represented by many renowned Japanese and Korean companies, which have contributed significantly towards its rapid growth. A major contributor to Malaysia's exports, the electrical and electronics industry is significant to the nation's economy.

items.title: The money tree, in its mould
items.caption: Two iron moulds and the tree they produced. Kelantan's tin pitis were cast in branching “money tree” forms, then snapped off coin by coin — a minting technique that arrived from Tang-dynasty China.
items.text: Acuan Pohon Pitis, Kelantan / 1904. Money Tree Mould, Kelantan / 1904. Most of Kelantan's tin pitis were made using moulds in the shape of a pitis tree. This method was probably introduced from China during the Tang Dynasty (618–906).

items.title: Cast, then snapped off
items.caption: The brass moulds up close — each dimple a coin, each stem a runner for molten tin. Mass production, 12th-century style.
items.text: Acuan Pohon Pitis, Kelantan / 1904. Money Tree Mould, Kelantan / 1904.

items.title: Ringgit Tongkat
items.caption: The trade-dollar map: dotted shipping lanes, tall ships and a press-here button that lights up each coin as it arrived in the Malay Archipelago.
items.text: Ringgit Tongkat — Dolar perak yang terkenal / The famous silver dollar. One Dollar, British Royal Mint, 1899. The British Trade Dollar was made valid for use in the British colonies on 2 February 1895, and it became popular in the Straits Settlements and the Malay States. The locals referred to these silver dollars as Ringgit Tongkat (Staff Ringgit), in reference to the trident in Britannia's hand. They were demonetised through the Straits Settlements (Coinage) Order 1903, effective 31 August 1904. However, the British Trade Dollars remained legal tender in the Hong Kong colony until 1 August 1935. Tekan di sini untuk melihat! / Press here to view!

items.title: Trade Dollars
items.caption: The gateway panel to the trade-dollar room. Before there was a ringgit, there was a rule: any silver crown of at least 415 grains at 90% fineness was money here.
items.text: Dolar Perdagangan / Trade Dollars. Various types of European coins were used for trade in the Malay Archipelago following the arrival of traders from Spain, Holland, Portugal and England in East India in the 16th Century. Thus, many types of crown silver coins from a number of nations were in circulation in the Malay Archipelago. The trading community accepted payment in any silver coins with a minimum weight of 415 grains, or 26.9 grams at a fineness of 900 (90% silver). Let's get to know more on the Trade Dollars used in the Malay Archipelago!

items.title: One Dollar, 1899
items.caption: Britannia with her trident, which is exactly why locals called it the Ringgit Tongkat — the staff ringgit.
items.text: Ringgit Tongkat — Dolar perak yang terkenal / The famous silver dollar. One Dollar, British Royal Mint, 1899.

items.title: One Dollar, British Hong Kong, 1866
items.caption: Queen Victoria on the obverse. Britain built a mint in Hong Kong specifically to produce trade dollars for the East — and deliberately matched the Mexican dollar's size and weight so merchants would accept it.
items.text: One Dollar, British Hong Kong, 1866. In 1866, the British government decided to build a mint in Hong Kong to produce trade dollars to be used in its colonies in the East and for trade in China. The Hong Kong Dollar was redesigned from the original British Crown to be similar to the Mexican Dollar in size and weight.

items.title: One Crown, Britain, 1804
items.caption: The British East India Company's crowns circulated in Penang, Malacca and Singapore and were accepted by traders — despite never once being granted legal tender status in the Straits Settlements.
items.text: One Crown, Britain, 1804. After the British began occupying Penang, Malacca and Singapore (in 1786, 1795 and 1819 respectively), the British East India Company circulated various types of British Crown money. The trading community accepted the British Crowns, even though they were never accorded legal tender status in the Straits Settlements. Salah satu dolar perak Eropah yang terawal / One of the earliest European Silver dollars.

items.title: Eight Reales, Spain, 1764
items.caption: The Pillar Dollar — “Pillar of Hercules,” known locally as Ringgit Tua, the old ringgit. The word ringgit itself means “jagged,” after the milled edge of these Spanish coins.
items.text: Eight Reales, Spain, 1764. The Spanish dollars used in the Malay Archipelago were the Spanish Cobs and the Spanish-Mexican silver dollars known as the Carolus Dollars and the Pillar Dollars. The Carolus Dollars, on their obverse bore portraits of the Spanish rulers Charles III, Charles IV, and later, Ferdinand VII. The Pillar Dollars on the other hand were inscribed with the words 'Pillar of Hercules' and were known as Ringgit Tua (Old Ringgit) in the 19th century.

items.title: Eight Reales or One Peso, Mexico, 1874
items.caption: The Mexican eagle on a cactus. Locals renamed it constantly — Ringgit Garuda, Ringgit Gerdun, Ringgit Burung — and the sunburst side became Ringgit Matahari, the sun ringgit.
items.text: Eight Reales or One Peso, Mexico, 1874. The one Peso silver coin depicted an eagle, with its wings spread open, perched on a cactus. In the Malay Archipelago, these coins had several nicknames including Ringgit Garuda (Mythical Eagle), Ringgit Gerdun, and Ringgit Burung (Bird). While the eight Reales silver coin which depicted a revolutionary's cap against a backdrop of sunrays on the obverse, were also known as Ringgit Janek or Ringgit Matahari (Sun).

items.title: The sun ringgit
items.caption: The liberty cap and sunburst that gave the coin its Malay nickname, photographed with the yellow disc of the exhibit swinging overhead.
items.text: Eight Reales or One Peso, Mexico, 1874.

items.title: One Yen, Meiji Japan
items.caption: Japan bought every minting machine Hong Kong had and started striking silver yen in 1870. In Terengganu the coin was known as Ringgit Muda — the young ringgit — to distinguish it from the Spanish Ringgit Tua.
items.text: One Yen, Japan Meiji, 1849–1912. When the Japanese government bought all the mints from Hong Kong, they began producing the one Meiji Yen silver coins in 1870 which weighed 416 grains each. They were widely distributed in the Malay states, especially in Terengganu. The locals referred to it as Ringgit Muda (Young Ringgit), to distinguish it from the Spanish Pillar Dollars, which were referred to as Ringgit Tua (Old Ringgit).

items.title: One Piastre, French Indo-China, 1898
items.caption: A coin that prints its own audit trail: weight and silver fineness stamped right on the obverse, so any merchant could verify it without trusting the issuer.
items.text: One Piastre, French Indo-China, 1898. The French Indo-China Piastre silver coins, displaying on the obverse their weights and silver fineness, were circulated in the Straits Settlements, the Malay States and in certain parts of Borneo. The first issue of the French Indo-China one Piastre coins weighed 27.215 grams each. After 1895, it was reduced to 27 grams each. Both issues had a fineness of 900 (90% silver).

items.title: Fineness, stamped on the face
items.caption: “TITRE 0.900 POIDS 27 GR.” — the proof-of-reserve of its day, minted into the metal itself.
items.text: INDO-CHINE FRANÇAISE — PIASTRE DE COMMERCE — TITRE 0.900, POIDS 27 GR. One Piastre, French Indo-China, 1898.

items.title: History of the Cheque
items.caption: A payment instrument older than the banks that issue it. Roman praescriptiones on wooden tablets, the Mauryan adesha, letters of credit in 9th-century Persia — and a Wesley Manufacturing cheque perforator from 1890s New York.
items.text: Sejarah Cek / History of the Cheque. A cheque is a written instruction directing a bank to pay an agreed amount of money to a beneficiary. It was developed as a method of payment to avoid having to carry around large amounts of money. Its origin is difficult to ascertain, though it is believed that cheques have been in use for over 1000 years. 100–1 SM/BCE: The ancient Romans used 'praescriptiones', a type of promissory note written in Latin on wooden tablets. 321–185 SM/BCE: The Maurya Empire in India used a commercial instrument called 'adesha', which was an order on a banker to pay an amount of money to a third party. 300 M/CE: Banks in Persian territory began issuing letters of credit called 'chak'. Tindakan Perlindungan Cek / Cheque Protection in Action: Perforation is another form of protection used against fraud. A cheque perforator punches small round holes that form perforated numerals as well as having perforations that are permanently inked. This cheque perforator was used during the 1890s and was manufactured by Wesley Manufacturing Company, New York.

items.title: Migration Towards ePayments
items.caption: The 2010s, in Bank Negara's own framing: a decade spent building regulatory structure, e-payment infrastructure and — the hardest part — public confidence.
items.text: Peralihan Kepada ePembayaran / Migration Towards ePayments. The 2010s was an important decade for building the regulatory structure, e-payment infrastructure and public confidence for the transition towards e-payments. There were many initiatives that have encouraged the switch from paper-based payments to e-payments, and facilitated wider coverage of e-payment infrastructure, such as POS terminals and mobile banking. These initiatives continue on today even as e-payments are becoming more widespread and accepted by the public at large.

items.title: Distribution Lifecycle of the Ringgit
items.caption: Follow one RM20 note from the distribution centre, through strangers' hands, and back again to be destroyed. “No two adventures are quite the same.”
items.text: Kitaran Hidup Pengedaran Wang Kertas Ringgit / Distribution Lifecycle of the Ringgit. Ever wondered what happens behind the scenes of that banknote you keep in your wallet? Follow a single banknote's journey through the country's various distribution channels, getting into the hands of a fellow stranger, being passed around in the real world, before ultimately being returned to a distribution centre, worn out and ready to finish its journey. In the end, a new RM20 banknote will replace its place in the world, but no two adventures are quite the same.

items.title: Safe Transfer of Money — in All Forms
items.caption: Cash? Card? Internet banking? Mobile payment? The panel is the museum's clearest statement of what a central bank thinks it is for: making sure value moves quickly, reliably and with minimum risk.
items.text: Pindahan Wang Yang Selamat — Dalam Semua Bentuk / Safe Transfer of Money — In All Forms. Cash? Card? Internet Banking? Mobile Payment? Today many of us have the option to make payments in various forms. Safe, reliable and efficient payment systems enable monetary transactions to be completed quickly and with minimum risk, thus facilitating economic activities and contributing to higher growth. Given the importance of the payment systems for the efficiency of the economy and the financial markets, Bank Negara Malaysia has a strong interest in ensuring that the payment systems in the country not only operate smoothly but are also being improved and developed to suit an increasingly more digital world. Do you want to know what some of the terms used here actually mean? Scan and find out!

items.title: Elements of a Cheque
items.caption: Eleven numbered parts of a single instrument — drawer, payee, date, amount in words and figures, MICR line, the “Account Payee Only” crossing. A protocol spec, in ink.
items.text: Elemen-elemen pada Sekeping Cek / Elements of a Cheque. 1. Name of the drawer bank. 2. The payee is the person to whom the cheque is made. 3. 'Account Payee Only' crossing is a directive to the collecting bank to pay into the account of the payee. 4. Date of the cheque. 5. The bearer is the person who presents the cheque to the bank; it is advisable to cross out 'or bearer' to avoid stolen cheques from being cashed. 6. The payment amount written in words — the same value will be written in the box beside it. 7. The signature of the drawer of the cheque. 8. Drawer's own account number. 9–11. MICR line: cheque number, bank and branch codes, account number. Many countries enacted laws to allow for cheque truncation, in which a physical cheque is converted into an electronic form for transmission to the paying bank or the clearing house.

items.title: 100-ton hydraulic coining press
items.caption: The machine that actually made the money. Bank Negara opened its own mint at Batu Tiga, Shah Alam in July 1971; before that, coins came from the Royal Mint in London and the Hamburg Mint.
items.text: 100 TON HYDRAULIC COINING PRESS, MODEL No. S 100T. Coin Minting.

items.title: Coin Minting
items.caption: Malaysia's first coins were struck on 12 June 1967. The 1967–69 coins came from the Royal Mint in London; the 1970 one-sen and twenty-sen pieces from Hamburg. Everything from 1 sen to 50 sen has been minted at home since July 1971.
items.text: Penempaan Duit Syiling / Coin Minting. With the introduction of the third series of coins in 2012, Bank Negara Malaysia marked its 45th year of coin issuance. Malaysian coins were first minted on 12 June 1967 with five denominations bearing the same motif. The $1 coin for normal circulation was issued on 1 May 1971. All coins dated 1967, 1968 and 1969 were struck at the Royal Mint, London. However, the 1 sen and 20 sen coins dated 1970 were produced at the Hamburg Mint in Germany. All coins in denominations from 1 sen to 50 sen have been minted locally since the opening of the Bank Negara Malaysia Mint in July 1971. Located at Batu Tiga in Shah Alam, Selangor, the Bank Negara Malaysia Mint was launched by the then Minister of Finance, Tun Tan Siew Sin. Since then, the Mint has not only been producing coins for circulation but it has also created many series of commemorative coins.

items.title: The first notes issued by the Bank
items.caption: $1, $5, $10, $50, $100 and $1,000, first series, 1967–1983. Every issue carried a tiger's-head watermark. The RM1,000 note showed the Parliament building on the back.
items.text: Wang Kertas Pertama Terbitan Bank Negara Malaysia / The First Notes Issued by the Bank. The First Series design, which had four issuances, was used from 1967 to 1983, covering the terms of office of the second and third Governors of Bank Negara Malaysia. The first three issuances were signed by Tun Ismail Ali, but only the fourth was signed by Tan Sri Abdul Aziz Hj Taha. All four issuances had a unique banknote security feature in the form of a tiger's head watermark. The original notes were printed in denominations of $1, $5, $10, $50, $100 and $1,000. All notes featured the image of the first King of Malaysia, His Majesty Tuanku Abdul Rahman ibni Al-marhum Tuanku Muhammad, as they do to this day. On the back, the $1,000 note carried a depiction of the Parliament building, while the smaller denominations featured a variety of designs with geometrical themes. Pengeluaran Mata Wang / Issuance of Currency. Authority to issue currency was vested in Bank Negara Malaysia by the Central Bank of Malaya Ordinance, 1958. However, Malaysian currency continued to be printed in Britain under the auspices of the Board of Commissioners of Currency Malaya and British Borneo until Bank Negara Malaysia assumed responsibility for currency production as well as issuance on 12 June 1967. The Malaysian currency is known as the Ringgit and it is made up of one hundred sen. The value of the Ringgit was originally fixed at 0.290299 grams of fine gold, while the exchange rate of the old Malayan Dollar was 2 shillings 4 pence. The old Malayan notes remained in circulation alongside the new Malaysian banknotes until 16 January 1969, when they were demonetised.

items.title: Specimens of the first series
items.caption: $5, $10, $50, $100 and $1,000, each stamped SPECIMEN, hanging in a red-lit case.
items.text: BANK NEGARA MALAYSIA — $5, $10, $50, $100, $1000 — SPECIMEN.

items.title: Unity of Design
items.caption: Six songket motifs from six banknotes, nested as concentric squares — the RM1,000 at the centre, the RM5 forming the border. Currency as textile, textile as national argument.

items.title: The motifs, named
items.caption: songket melur (RM1,000), teluk berantai (RM500), pucuk rebung pedada (RM100), pucuk rebung (RM50), pucuk rebung berjuang (RM10), pucuk rebung lawi ayam (RM5) — the last four from the fourth series, themed “Distinctively Malaysia.”
items.text: Unity of Design. This is a unique design featuring six distinct songket motifs found on Malaysian banknotes. Arranged in a concentric square pattern the well-matched motifs create a harmonious and aesthetically pleasing piece of art. At the centre is the songket melur pattern, found on RM1,000 banknote. The next layer features the teluk berantai motif, embedded on a RM500 banknote. Both the RM1,000 and RM500 are banknotes printed during the second currency series. The third layer depicts the pucuk rebung pedada motif, derived from a RM100 banknote. This is followed by the basic pucuk rebung pattern as seen on RM50 banknote. The fifth layer in the arrangement shows the pucuk rebung berjuang motif, originating from a RM10 banknote. Decorating the outer border is the pattern of pucuk rebung lawi ayam, found on RM5 banknote. All motifs for RM100, RM50, RM10 and RM5 are exclusive patterns in the fourth currency series, themed 'Distinctively Malaysia'.

items.title: “The World Embraces Islamic Finance”
items.caption: The threshold into the Islamic Finance Gallery — a lit cylinder wrapped in geometric strapwork, black floor reflecting it back.
items.text: Kewangan Islam Menjangkaui Dunia / The World Embraces Islamic Finance.

items.title: Galeri Kewangan Islam
items.caption: The gallery's own statement of scope, wrapped around a column: a body of practice that began as religious obligation and is now a trillion-dollar industry.
items.text: Galeri Kewangan Islam / Islamic Finance Gallery. The basis of Islamic Finance lies in the principles of the Shariah, or Islamic Law. Islamic finance has undergone rapid growth and transformation. From an industry initially intended to fulfil the religious obligations of the Muslim community, it is now a trillion-dollar industry driven by well-defined business considerations and profit optimisation, whilst upholding Islamic principles.

items.title: Basic Concepts and Principles
items.caption: Six values that any Shariah-compliant transaction is meant to embody. Read them next to a whitepaper and the overlap is uncomfortable and interesting in equal measure.
items.text: Konsep dan Prinsip Asas / Basic Concepts and Principles. Financial transactions based on Shariah principles seek to embody and uphold the following intrinsic values: Economic well-being for all · Fairness and justice for all · Fair distribution of wealth · Honesty and transparency · Mutual cooperation, solidarity and harmony · Freedom to enter into contracts. QUICK FACT: Majallah Al-Ahkam Al-Adliyyah (The Mejelle) is the first codification of rulings of Hanafi school of law by Ottoman authorities in the 19th century. Amongst its content are rulings on Islamic financial transactions and obligations in line with Shariah principles. All dealings within the Islamic financial system are based on concepts of mutual consent and pursuit of lawful objectives. Muslims are required to avoid any contract that includes elements of riba (interest), gharar (uncertainty due to deception or ignorance) or maysir (gambling and other games of chance) or any activity strictly prohibited in Islam.

items.title: A handwritten Quran from Uzbekistan, 1354
items.caption: Open to Al-Baqarah 282 — the longest verse in the Quran, and the one that makes writing down a debt contract obligatory. A 1354 manuscript arguing for immutable, witnessed records of financial agreements.
items.text: Al-Quran tulisan tangan dari Uzbekistan, 1354 / Handwritten Quran from Uzbekistan, 1354. Verse 282 of Al-Baqarah is the longest in the Holy Quran concerning lending money or financing. The verse makes it obligatory to write a contract for financing, which is to be witnessed by a trustworthy person. The emphasis is on the need for writing down the financing contract regardless of how small the amount along with the repayment date. Quran Translation: “O believers! When you contract a debt from one another for a fixed period, put it (its amount and period of repayment) in writing. And let a scribe write it down between you justly (truthfully), and no scribe should refuse to write as Allah has taught him…” (Surah al-Baqarah: Verse 282)

items.title: Verse 282, up close
items.caption: The label in full. “Put it in writing… and let a scribe write it down between you justly.” A seven-hundred-year-old case for the append-only ledger.
items.text: Al-Quran tulisan tangan dari Uzbekistan, 1354 / Handwritten Quran from Uzbekistan, 1354. Ayat 282 Surah Al-Baqarah ini adalah ayat terpanjang di dalam Al-Quran yang menjurus kepada pinjaman wang atau pembiayaan.

items.title: The Prohibition on Riba
items.caption: Riba is forbidden to protect people from injustice and exploitation — a response to pre-Islamic Meccan money-lending, where a lender could unilaterally increase the debt if a borrower missed a payment.
items.text: Larangan ke atas Riba (Bunga/Faedah) / The Prohibition on Riba (Usury / Interest). Riba is forbidden in order to safeguard people from injustice and exploitation. The restriction on making profit through riba was in response to oppressive pre-Islamic money-lending practices in Mecca, which allowed a lender to unilaterally increase the sum owed if the borrower failed to make repayment in time. QUICK FACT: The literal meaning of the word riba is 'to increase'. Enrichment through riba violates the fundamental principle that a Muslim should only profit through his own efforts, instead of charging the premium on the loan.

items.title: Islamic Civilization: Trade and Finance
items.caption: Ten teal panels tracing how Islamic trade practice spread — coins, souks, contracts, coffee, ghubar numerals.
items.text: Tamadun Islam: Perdagangan dan Kewangan / Islamic Civilization: Trade and Finance.

items.title: Contracts as commandment
items.caption: The middle panel is the one worth stopping at: trade mattered so much that Muslim rulers created contract law, and “honour your contracts” arrives in the Quran as an order, not advice.
items.text: It is believed that two giant gold Islamic coins existed in the early 1600s, one of these coins was 8 inches (20 cm) in diameter and weighed in at 26.5 pounds (12 kg) of pure gold. The Islamic Empire significantly contributed to globalization during the Islamic Golden Age, when the knowledge, trade and economies from many previously isolated regions and civilizations began integrating through contacts with Muslim explorers and traders. Trade was so important that Muslim rulers created contracts, loans and more, which still influence trade today. As written in the Quran, 'O Believers! Honor your contracts' (5:1) which means honouring agreements is given as a commandment. Shopping for food, spices (cinnamon, cassia, cardamom, ginger and tumeric), books and other goods was done at an open-air market called a souk. Medieval Islamic economics appears to simulate proto-capitalism. Some scholars have also found a number of parallels between Islamic economic jurisprudence and social justice, including the Islamic ideas of zakat and riba.

items.title: Dinar, dirham and the port of Mocha
items.caption: The first Islamic coins with Arabic inscriptions were struck by Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan (685–705). The words dinar and dirham are themselves borrowed — from the Greek denarion and drachm.
items.text: The first Caliph to create the first Islamic coin was Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, who ruled from 685 to 705. These were also the first gold coins to carry an Arabic inscription. 'Mocha' is both the name of a kind of coffee bean and the name of a port in Yemen that was the centre of the coffee trade from the 15th to 17th centuries. Traders in the Muslim world used gold and silver coins called 'Dinars' and 'Dirhams', as international currency. 'Dinars' were borrowed via the Syriac 'Dinara' from the Greek 'Denarion' while 'Dirham' comes from the name of a Greek coin, the 'Drachm'. Islamic Empire (including the Rashidun, Umayyad, Abbasid and Fatimid) caliphates as the world's leading extensive economic power throughout the 7th–13th centuries trade networks extended from the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea in the west to the Indian Ocean and China Sea in the east. Arabic numerals were also known as Ghubari numbers because Muslims initially used dust (ghubar) boards for calculations.

items.title: Weighing Scales and Box, Safavid Iran
items.caption: A 16th-century travelling assay kit: two sets of scales and a set of weights in a carved wooden box, for verifying gold, silver, jewellery and precious stones on the spot.
items.text: Kotak dan Skala Penimbang, Dinasti Safawid, Iran, Abad ke-16 / Weighing Scales and Box, Safavid Dynasty, Iran, 16th century. These scales were used for weighing valuable items, such as gold, silver, jewellery and precious stones, which were essential to the pursuit of trade and commerce. They are housed in a fine carved wooden box, which contains two scales of different sizes and a set of weights.

items.title: Early Practice in Islamic Finance
items.caption: Mudarabah — profit-sharing — predates Islam and was endorsed by the Prophet Muhammad. By the 9th century, Arab traders could cash a cheque in Baghdad against funds held in China.
items.text: Early Practice in Islamic Finance. Islam is a dynamic religion that is able to address the needs of people at any time and place. Prior to the revelation of Islam, Arab traders had already practised mudarabah (profit sharing). Prophet Muhammad endorsed mudarabah as it was deemed to be consistent with Islamic principles. Further advancement in Islamic commercial practices was seen by innovations in payment methods. Instead of cash, sakk (cheque) and hawalah for assignment of debt (similar to modern bills of exchange) were used. From the 9th century, Arab traders were able to cash cheques in China to access their funds in Baghdad. Islam brought change to the traditional wealth distribution mechanism by the encouragement of waqf (endowment) which enables individuals to create trust funds for charitable purposes. Examples of projects initiated by waqf include the Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque in Fez, Morocco (established 859 AD) and Al-Azhar University (established 971 AD) in Cairo, Egypt. Institutions like Bayt al-Mal, which means public treasury, were established to collect taxes which were used to pay for public works and infrastructure and to provide charity for the poor. QUICK FACT: The University of Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, is generally considered to be the oldest continuously operating degree-granting university in the world.

items.title: Empire and Invention
items.caption: From the 7th century to European colonialism, Islamic empires dominated world trade — and the wealth funded the Umayyad Mosque, the Alhambra and the Taj Mahal. Ibn Sina theorised germ transmission in the 10th century.
items.text: Empire and Invention. From the 7th century until the rise of European colonialism, Islamic empires dominated world trade. The wealth and power of Muslim rulers resulted in the flourishing of art, culture and architecture, providing wonders such as the Grand Umayyad Mosque in Damascus, Syria, the Alhambra in Granada, Spain and the Taj Mahal in Agra, India. QUICK FACT: In the 10th century, the Persian physician and philosopher Ibn Sina or Avicenna (980–1037), theorised that germs and lack of hygiene caused disease, a fact that was disregarded by western medicine until the 18th century. Many discoveries in the fields of medicine and astronomy were attributed to Muslim scholars whose achievements ranged from differentiating between stars and planets to developing anaesthetics.

items.title: Astrolabe and manuscript, 16th century
items.caption: The instrument that made long-distance trade navigable. Its value to merchants, the label says flatly, was “beyond calculation.”
items.text: Manuskrip Astrolab, Abad ke-16 / Astrolabe Manuscript, 16th Century. An astrolabe is an elaborate instrument, historically used by astronomers, navigators and astrologers. Its many uses include locating and predicting the positions of the sun, moon, planets and stars, determining local time given local latitude or vice-versa, as well as surveying and triangulation. Its value for merchants and international trade was beyond calculation. This 16th century manuscript shows astronomers working with an armillary sphere to create charts of the stars which were then turned into astrolabes.

items.title: The armillary sphere
items.caption: Astronomers climbing a wooden armillary sphere in a 16th-century illumination — the observational work behind every astrolabe.

items.title: Brass astrolabe
items.caption: The object itself: pierced brass rete, rotating alidade, month names running around the limb. A handheld analogue computer for the sky.

items.title: Al-Idrisi's world, lit from below
items.caption: The map case in the Islamic Finance Gallery — Edrisi's Weltkarte above, the Tabula Rogeriana glowing on a lightbox below, with MOROCCO, SICILY and TURKEY etched along the rim.
items.text: Introduction — The Golden Age of Muslim Civilisation, that is from the 7th century onwards brought together men and women from different faiths and cultures to work together to create thousands of inventions and discoveries that changed the world. Stretching over three continents, from Spain and northern Africa through the Middle East to Indonesia and China, Muslim civilisation contributed to the advances in science, mathematics, medicine, technology, architecture, geography, economics, finance, trade and in many other areas of human life. Among the inventions were camera obscura, surgical instruments, windmills, astrolabes, mechanical clocks and many more.

items.title: Hukum Kanun Melaka
items.caption: The 16th-century legal code of Malacca. Of its 44 sections, sections 29 to 34 are the commercial ones: business ethics, transaction of goods, the condition of goods for sale, acceptable conduct between buyer and seller.
items.text: Hukum Kanun Melaka. The formal legal text encompassing matters of social conduct as well as official rules and laws were stipulated in traditional 16th century Melaka society. These include the Undang-Undang Melaka (Laws of Malacca), also called the Hukum Kanun Melaka and Risalat Hukum Kanun, and the Undang-Undang Laut Melaka (the Maritime Laws of Malacca). The rules were formed through the evolution of three main influences, namely the non-indigenous Hindu/Buddhist tradition, Islamic jurisdiction and indigenous 'adat'. The Hukum Kanun Melaka contains 44 sections of rules, with sections 29 to 34 being the most related to business and financial practices. The book explains business ethics, transaction of goods, the condition of goods on sale and acceptable buyer and seller conduct, which are based on Shariah or Islamic law.

items.title: The Tabula Rogeriana, explained
items.caption: Al-Idrisi spent fifteen years making this atlas for King Roger II of Sicily, in 1154. He presented it engraved on a disc of solid silver two metres across. For three centuries it was the reference — for Ibn Battuta, Ibn Khaldun, Piri Reis and Columbus.
items.text: Tabula Rogeriana. The Tabula Rogeriana was drawn by Muslim geographer and cartographer Mohammed Al-Idrisi for King Roger II of Sicily in 1154. Al-Idrisi spent 15 years creating 70 maps for the atlas of King Roger II based on his own personal knowledge and experience with information from older maps, particularly Roman charts and Ptolemy. He also collected reports from seafaring Muslim merchants, Norman voyagers and Christian scholars and used that information to assemble the most accurate map of its time. Al-Idrisi is said to have presented the map to King Roger II on a disc of solid silver two metres in diameter. The map was also made into manuscript form, a few of which survive today. For three centuries, geographers used Al-Idrisi's unaltered maps and the work of Al-Idrisi inspired some of the world's greatest explorers, scholars and cartographers including Ibn Battuta, Ibn Khaldun, Piri Re'is, and Christopher Columbus.

items.title: The map itself
items.caption: Backlit on the case floor — blue seas, red rivers, and the Malay Peninsula reduced to a scatter of islands off to one edge.

items.title: Edrisi's Weltkarte, 1789
items.caption: A German edition of Al-Idrisi's 12th-century world map. The original was drawn with south at the top; this version flips it for European readers. The Malay Peninsula, Java, Sumatra and Sri Lanka come out as a jumble of islands.
items.text: Edrisi's Welkarte, German/Germany, 1789, Mohammed Al-Idrisi. A German version of Al-Idrisi's important 12th century map of the World. Originally drawn with south at the top of the page but for the simplicity of comprehension, this version from an unidentified work has been presented in conventional form — with north at the top of the page. By providing information of England, Russia and Finmark, the map depicts the best available geographical information known to inhabitants of the Mediterranean region during the period. The horn of Africa has been extended to the Far East, becoming a close neighbour of Southeast Asia. The Malay Peninsula, Java, Sumatra and Sri Lanka have been reduced to a jumble of islands.

items.title: Malacca's commercial code, open
items.caption: The manuscript itself, in Jawi script — a working legal text from the port city that made the Straits the busiest waterway in the world.
items.text: Hukum Kanun Melaka. The Hukum Kanun Melaka contains 44 sections of rules, with sections 29 to 34 being the most related to business and financial practices.

items.title: Islamic Coins — Abbasid to Mughal
items.caption: Four dynasties across nine centuries: Abbasid 814 AD, Buyid 1009, Ayyubid 1234, Mughal 1733. The coins themselves were away for conservation; the museum left the outlines and a note.
items.text: Duit Syiling Islam / Islamic Coins. 1. Dinasti Abbasiyah, Tahun 198 H / 814 TM (Abbasid, 198 AH / 814 AD). 2. Dinasti Buyid, 399 H / 1009 TM (399 AH / 1009 AD). 3. Dinasti Ayyubid, 631 H / 1234 TM (631 AH / 1234 AD). 4. Dinasti Mughal, 1146 H / 1733 TM (1146 AH / 1733 AD). Duit syiling ini dikeluarkan sementara bagi tujuan konservasi / The coins are temporarily removed for conservation work.

items.title: Out for conservation
items.caption: An honest, unglamorous museum moment: an empty case, a printed placeholder, and a label explaining exactly why.
items.text: Duit Syiling Islam / Islamic Coins — The coins are temporarily removed for conservation work.

items.title: Islamic Currency and Coinage
items.caption: Caliph Umar Al-Khattab fixed the exchange rate in the early 7th century: 7 dinars to 10 dirhams, the dinar at 4.25 grams and the dirham at 3.0. A monetary standard, written down and held.
items.text: Islamic Currency and Coinage. Early Muslim rulers used gold (dinar) and silver (dirham) as the standard of value for their currency. The introduction of standardised coins and currency throughout the Islamic trade routes diminished the reliance on barter trade and provided merchants with a reliable system for pricing their goods. QUICK FACT: Under the Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, Islamic coins were inscribed with Arabic script to differentiate them from Greek and Persian coins in circulation. In the early 7th century, Caliph Umar Al-Khattab standardised the currency exchange between dinar and dirham, with 7 dinars equivalent to 10 dirhams. The weight of the dinar was set at 4.25 grams and dirham at 3.0 grams. The first Dinar was minted in Damascus, Syria (694 AD) and later in Basra, Iraq and Al-Fustat, Egypt.

items.title: Minting Kit, 19th century
items.caption: Three bronze crucibles for carrying molten metal, bronze scissors for trimming coin edges, a steel minting mould and two stone seals for making trading tablets. A mint you could carry.
items.text: Alat Penempa / Minting Kit. This 19th century minting kit possibly from Central Asia includes three bronze containers for transporting melted metal, a pair of bronze scissors for cutting the edges of coins, a steel minting mould and two stone seals to create tablets for trading purposes.

items.title: Scissors, crucibles, seals
items.caption: The tools close up. Everything you need to issue money, small enough to fit in a saddlebag.

items.title: Ungku Aziz's memorandum, 1959
items.caption: “Rancangan Membaiki Ekonomi Bakal-bakal Haji” — a plan to improve the economy of prospective pilgrims. Malays were selling land and livestock to fund the Hajj and returning home poorer. The memo led to Lembaga Tabung Haji in 1969.
items.text: Memorandum Rancangan Membaiki Ekonomi Bakal-bakal Haji / Memorandum to Improve the Economy of People going for Haj. The historic memorandum was proposed by Royal Professor Ungku Aziz to the Malaysian government in December 1959. It begins with two verses from the Qur'an — the first “perform the Haj and Umrah” and “cooperate in righteousness and piety” — summarises the importance of establishing an official body to assist Muslims in completing their Haj. Through in-depth research in the early 1950s, it was found that the main purpose of domestic savings for the majority of Malays was to complete the Haj. Unfortunately, their method of savings could be harmful economically as it included the selling of land, jewellery or livestock, which would leave the pilgrims to suffer financially after their return from Mecca. Lembaga Urusan Tabung Haji (LUTH), which was officially established in 1969, provided the opportunity for all Muslims to save gradually for their Haj as well as enabling them to invest and participate in economic and financial activities that are beneficial and in accordance with Islamic principles.

items.title: “Penubuhan Bank Islam” — the founding report
items.caption: A classified green-bound committee report and its covering letter. The paperwork that produced Bank Islam Malaysia and the Islamic Banking Act 1983.
items.text: SULIT — PENUBUHAN BANK ISLAM: Laporan Jawatankuasa Pemandu Kebangsaan Bank Islam. Report from National Steering Committee on the Establishment of Bank Islam.

items.title: From Tabung Haji to Bank Islam
items.caption: The chain of institutions, spelled out: Tabung Haji (1969) proved the demand, the National Steering Committee (1981) wrote the guidelines, and the Islamic Banking Act 1983 came into force in April 1983.
items.text: Laporan Jawatankuasa Pemandu Kebangsaan bagi Penubuhan Bank Islam / Report from National Steering Committee on the Establishment of Bank Islam. The establishment of Islamic banking in Malaysia was a gradual process, which was a result of collective knowledge from preceding Islamic financial institutions around the world. Lembaga Tabung Haji, established in 1969, was the first institution to practise the concept of Islamic transaction. Demand for more Islamic-based products was high, which prompted the government to establish the National Steering Committee in 1981 to provide an operating guideline for merchant banks, founded on Shariah principles. Feedbacks from the National Steering Committee paved the way in establishing an Islamic bank in Malaysia. The government endorsed the Islamic Banking Act 1983 (IBA), which was implemented in April 1983.

items.title: Evolution of Arabic numerals
items.caption: Glowing rows of digits mutating from Indian Brahmi through Arabic into the shapes on your keyboard. The reason zero and positional notation reached Europe at all was trade.
items.text: Evolusi angka Arab / Evolution of Arabic numerals. Arabic numerals are known by many names, including Indian numerals and Indo-Arabic numerals. These ten digits (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 0) are descended from the numeral system developed by Indian mathematicians, in which a sequence of digits such as '975' is read as a number. The Indian numerals were adopted by Persian and Arab mathematicians in India, and from there passed on to the Arabs further west. From there, they were transmitted to Europe in the Middle Ages when they were eventually welcomed as an easy alternative to the clumsy system of Roman numerals. The use of Arabic numerals spread around the world through trade, books and colonialism. Today they are the most common symbolic representation of numbers in existence.

items.title: Tughra Seal and Suftaja
items.caption: Two answers to the same problem — how do you make a promise portable? The Ottoman tughra authenticated documents; the Qajar suftaja moved money without moving money.
items.text: Mohor Tughra, Ottoman, Turki, Batu akik / Tughra Seal, Ottoman Turkey, agate stone. Tughras were the official signature and seal of the Ottoman Sultans representing power and supreme authority. They were often used to legalise official documents. However they were also seen on coins, flags, stamps, official buildings, ships, mosques and palaces as a symbol of sovereignty. Tughras also have long been appreciated as fine works of art. Suftaja, Dinasti Qajar, Iran / Suftaja, Qajar Dynasty, Iran. In the early days of Islam, a suftaja, which is a bill of exchange or letter of credit, was used to expedite long-distance payments or fund transfers. The suftaja would be issued by one party to be used by the bearer, to pay another party, with a monetary agreement beforehand. The suftaja helped to avoid the risk of transporting money.

items.title: A suftaja, in the case
items.caption: The instrument itself: 500 Toman, Qajar Iran. A bearer note that let a merchant settle a debt a thousand miles away without carrying a single coin across a desert.
items.text: Suftaja, Qajar Dynasty, Iran. In the early days of Islam, a suftaja, which is a bill of exchange or letter of credit, was used to expedite long-distance payments or fund transfers. 500 Toman (Iranian Currency) equals to 500 Gheran (Old Iranian Currency).

items.title: Wadiah passbook and the first Shariah credit card
items.caption: A Bank Islam savings book based on the wadiah (safekeeping) contract, and the Bank Islam Card — the first purely Shariah-contract credit card in Malaysia, free of riba and gharar, and the first Malaysian card on SMART chip technology.
items.text: Buku akaun simpanan Bank Islam / Bank Islam Saving Account Book. Bank Islam offers Wadiah Savings facility to save money. Based on Wadiah contract, this facility provides hassle-free safekeeping of money and allows easy access for withdrawals, whenever needed. Wadiah means custody or safekeeping. In a Wadiah arrangement, you will deposit cash or other assets in a bank for safekeeping. The bank guarantees the safety of the items kept by it. Kad Bank Islam / Bank Islam Card. Bank Islam Card (BIC) is the first purely Shariah contract based credit card to be offered to Muslims and non-Muslims in Malaysia. This card is completely free from any 'riba' or 'gharar' element. BIC is also the first credit card in Malaysia using the SMART chip technology, which adopts high security level in a credit card.

items.title: Malaysia: The Next Frontier
items.caption: The Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009 explicitly codifies a dual financial system — “The financial system in Malaysia shall consist of the conventional financial system and the Islamic financial system.” Two systems, one country, by statute.
items.text: Malaysia: The Next Frontier. Malaysia is at the forefront of the development of a comprehensive Islamic financial system. The country now has Islamic banking institutions, takaful (Islamic insurance) and re-takaful operators, a vibrant Islamic money market and a dynamic Islamic capital market which are supported by a robust regulatory and supervisory framework. QUICK FACT: The Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009 explicitly codifies the duality of the Malaysian financial system which 'The financial system in Malaysia shall consist of the conventional financial system and the Islamic financial system'. Following the successful establishment of the first Islamic bank in 1983, conventional banks in Malaysia were allowed to offer Islamic banking services in parallel with conventional banking products, thereby creating a dual banking system. Syarikat Takaful Malaysia Berhad, the first takaful operator in Malaysia, commenced operations in 1985.

items.title: Development of Takaful
items.caption: Mutual insurance, described by the 19th-century scholar Ibn Abidin: a merchant leases a ship, pays a sum called sukra, and is compensated if the cargo is lost. Everyone pays a tabarru — a donation — into a common fund.
items.text: Development of Takaful. In Islamic history, the concept of takaful or Islamic insurance was first mentioned by the 19th century Muslim scholar Ibn Abidin, who wrote of a merchant who leased a ship for trading activities. In addition, the merchant also paid a sum of money known as sukra or premium to a person who, in return, would compensate the merchant in the event of the cargo being damaged or destroyed during the voyage. This was practised in the Ottoman Empire. The essence of takaful involves a group of participants agreeing to compensate each other against a defined loss or damage. Each participant contributes a tabarru or donation into a common fund which is managed by a third party, who is the takaful operator. Should there be a calamity befalling one of the participants, compensation will be paid from the common fund. QUICK FACT: A special task force was established by the Government of Malaysia in 1982 to study the viability of setting up an Islamic insurance company. Following the recommendations of the Task Force, the Takaful Act was enacted in 1984.

items.title: Creating an Islamic Money Market
items.caption: Malaysia's Islamic money market turns over roughly RM1 billion a day. The instrument list on the wall reads like a parallel financial universe: GII, MITB, BNMN-i, Cagamas Mudharabah Bonds, Sukuk BNM Ijarah.
items.text: Creating an Islamic Money Market. The role of financial markets is to bring together providers and users of funds. Financial markets provide financial institutions with both long and short term financing facilities. These markets also act as a channel for monetary policy. QUICK FACT: To ensure stability whilst maintaining the funds and liquidity of the Islamic banking system, the Islamic money market allows banks with a surplus to channel funds to banks with a deficit based on Shariah principles. Malaysia's Islamic Money Market is one of the most advanced in the world, with average trading turnover of RM1 billion a day. Among the major Islamic money market instruments are the Government Investment Issue (GII), Malaysian Islamic Treasury Bills (MITB), Bank Negara Monetary Notes-I (BNMN-i), Cagamas Mudharabah Bonds (SMC), Islamic Accepted Bills (IAB), Islamic Negotiable Instruments (INI), Islamic Private Debt Securities (IPDS), Ar Rahnu Agreement-i (RA-i), and Sukuk BNM Ijarah (SBNMI).

items.title: The landmark sukuk, 2002
items.caption: A gold-domed trophy holding a USD 600 million certificate. On 25 June 2002 Malaysia issued the world's first international Islamic sovereign securities — a five-year sovereign sukuk that other countries then copied.
items.text: Detik Penting Sukuk / Landmark Sukuk. On 25 June 2002, the Malaysian Government issued an international five-year sovereign sukuk (Islamic bond) at USD 600 million, the first international Islamic sovereign securities offering. The landmark sukuk by the Malaysian Government set the pace for the issuance of several sovereign sukuks by other countries. Malaysia Global Sukuk Inc. — USD 600,000,000 Global Islamic Securities due 2007, HSBC.

items.title: The Sukuk Timeline
items.caption: A wall-height chronology of firsts, 1990 to 2015 — first ringgit sukuk by a foreign non-Islamic company, first global sovereign sukuk, first Emas sukuk, first sukuk by a UK-owned multinational (Tesco Malaysia).
items.text: SUKUK TIMELINE. 1990: First ringgit sukuk issuance by foreign-owned, non-Islamic company RM125 million — Shell MDS Sdn Bhd. 2001: First global corporate sukuk USD150 million — Kumpulan Guthrie. 2002: First global sovereign sukuk USD600 million — Government of Malaysia. 2004: First ringgit sukuk issuance by supranational agency RM500 million — International Finance Corporation / World Bank. 2005: Innovative sukuk structure, Sukuk al-Amanah Li al-Istithmar RM2.05 billion — Cagamas MBS Bhd. 2006: First exchangeable sukuk USD750 million — Khazanah Nasional Bhd. 2007: First sukuk issuance by a Japanese-owned multinational corporation RM400 million — AEON Credit Services. First hybrid sukuk in the world RMB billion — Nucleus Avenue Malakoff Corporation. First sukuk issuance by a UK-owned multinational corporation RM3.5 billion — Tesco Malaysia. 2008: First ringgit sukuk by a multilateral development institution RM1 billion — Islamic Development Bank. 2009: First Emas sukuk USD1.5 billion — Petroliam Nasional Bhd. 2010: First Emas sukuk by a Japanese company USD100 million — Nomura Holdings. First Singapore dollar denominated Emas sukuk SGD1.5 billion — Khazanah Nasional Bhd. 2011: First offshore RMB sukuk RMB500 million — Khazanah Nasional Bhd. 2012: Single largest sukuk issuance RM30.6 billion — Projek Lebuhraya Utara Selatan (PLUS) Bhd. First exchangeable sukuk with negative yield USD357.8 million — Khazanah Nasional Bhd. Innovative sukuk structure using airtime voucher as underlying asset in foreign currency RM61.0 billion — Axiata Bhd. 2014: First Japanese yen sukuk JPY2.5 billion — Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ. 2015: Longest USD tenured sukuk by a sovereign (30 years) USD500 million — Government of Malaysia.

items.title: 1955–1974: Planting the Seeds
items.caption: The Bank's journey started five years before the Bank existed — a small, determined group working with almost no blueprints, building a central bank for a country that was still becoming one.
items.text: Menyemai Benih: Permulaan Bank Negara Malaysia / Planting the Seeds: The Inception of Bank Negara Malaysia, 1955–1974. Bank Negara Malaysia's journey started five years prior to its establishment. Economic experts examined and envisioned a future central bank for the country as it moved closer to independence. With limited blueprints, Bank Negara Tanah Melayu, consisting of a small but determined group of individuals, began playing its role in nation-building.

items.title: 1980–1993: Building Momentum
items.caption: The country in its adolescence — manufacturing rising, dependence on rubber and tin falling, and a central bank trying to stay ahead of an economy changing faster than its own institutions.
items.text: Membina Momentum: Era Progresif Bank Negara Malaysia / Building Momentum: The Bank's Progressive Era, 1980–1993. The country, now in its adolescent phase, had witnessed a burgeoning manufacturing industry, which reduced its dependency on rubber and tin exports. In this evolving global economic landscape, the Bank had to maintain a constant vigilance, staying ahead of the curve to ensure a solid foundation for our nation's prosperity.

items.title: 1994–1999: Foundational Facelift
items.caption: Strong institutions, a vibrant economy — and then the Asian Financial Crisis. The panel's phrase for what the Bank became is worth keeping: “a beacon of light as the country entered unchartered waters.”
items.text: Pembaharuan: Ketangkasan Dalam Menangani Cabaran / Foundational Facelift: Resilience Through Challenges, 1994–1999. With strong institutions in place and a vibrant economy underway, the 1990s was mostly a time for improvements in Bank Negara Malaysia's structure and systems. However, the decade was challenged by the Asian Financial Crisis where Bank Negara Malaysia was tasked to become a beacon of light as the country entered unchartered waters for recovery.

items.title: Health Checks on Financial Institutions
items.caption: The supervision panel — license, regulate, inspect, and if necessary investigate. A Risk Based Supervisory Framework, off-site surveillance, on-site visits, follow-up communications.
items.text: Health Checks on Financial Institutions. One of the most important duties of Bank Negara Malaysia is to ensure that the nation's public and private financial institutions serve their customers honestly and efficiently. To this end, Bank Negara Malaysia is empowered under a variety of Acts to license, regulate, inspect, and if necessary, investigate the activities of banks, insurance companies and a wide range of other financial institutions to ensure sound and prudent conduct of their operations. A Risk Based Supervisory Framework is used to assess and monitor the performance of licensed financial institutions in major areas of potential problems including credit, market, liquidity and operational risks. These important tasks are performed by Bank Negara Malaysia specialists, who are responsible for a system of supervisory planning, off-site surveillance, on-site visits and follow-up communications.

items.title: The Logo's Inspiration
items.caption: In 1964 the Bank's first Malaysian Governor, Tun Ismail Mohamed Ali, chose the gold Kelantan kijang coin as the basis for the logo — partly because, unlike most early Malay coins that carried only Jawi script, this one carried an image.
items.text: Inspirasi Logo / The Logo's Inspiration. The Bank Negara Malaysia logo was inspired by a Kelantanese coin of the 13th–16th century. In 1964, the first Malaysian Governor of Bank Negara Malaysia, Tun Ismail Mohamed Ali, selected the gold Kelantan Kijang coin for its value and prestige. Also, unlike most early coins from the Malay Peninsula, which had only Jawi script, the gold Kijang coin featured the barking deer. Tun Ismail then commissioned a famous Malaysian sculptor, the late Abdul Wahab Haji Tahir, to create a symbol based on a stylised representation of the barking deer shown on the coin.

items.title: Our Mandate
items.caption: Carved into a stone wall, quoted from the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009: promote monetary stability and financial stability conducive to the sustainable growth of the Malaysian economy. That is the whole job.
items.text: Mandat Kami / Our Mandate. The principal objects of the Bank shall be to promote monetary stability and financial stability conducive to the sustainable growth of the Malaysian economy. — Excerpt from Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009.

items.title: 1959: the first annual report
items.caption: Seventeen pages. Sixty-seven staff. The Bank's first annual report, published the same year the Bank was born — and the start of a transparency tradition that still runs.
items.text: 1959: Laporan Tahunan Pertama / 1959: The First Annual Report. The Central Bank of Malaya's first annual report marked an important milestone in the Bank's history. Published in 1959, the same year the bank was born, it revealed how a young nation planned to secure its financial future. Unlike today's thick reports, this one was only 17 pages, short and straightforward but packed with ambition. It outlined the Bank's establishment, principal objectives, banking operations, commercial banking, annual accounts, and its staff. Can you guess how many staff were employed at that time? It was only 67! This humble report started a tradition of transparency that continues today.

items.title: The Ordinance, 1958
items.caption: His Majesty's Government Gazette, open at the Central Bank of Malaya Ordinance 1958 — passed 23 October 1958, the law that created a central bank with powers to issue currency, regulate banks and advise the government.
items.text: Ordinan Bank Negara Tanah Melayu 1958 / Central Bank of Malaya Ordinance 1958. This historic law established a central bank with powers to issue currency, regulate banks, and advise the government, ensuring stability and trust in a growing economy. The Ordinance was later revised as the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 1958 (Act 519, Revised 1994), strengthening the Bank's role for decades to come. Fifteen years later, in 2009, the act was repealed and replaced by the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009. Laporan Bank Antarabangsa bagi Pemulihan dan Pembangunan / The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and Central Banking in Malaya. Back in 1955, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) was asked how a young country should manage monetary stability, regulate credit, and support economic growth. Two experts, G. M. Watson and Sir Sydney Caine, helped shape these ideas. This report was more than just words — it gave Malaya the power to control its own financial future.

items.title: Opening day, 26 January 1959
items.caption: The official launch programme book. The Bank began operating out of part of the PWD Selangor building near Dataran Merdeka, and didn't move into its own RM9.6 million headquarters on Jalan Dato Onn until 1970.
items.text: Buku Program Pelancaran Rasmi: Kenangan Bersejarah / The Official Launch Programme Book: A Keepsake of History. On 26 January 1959, Bank Negara Tanah Melayu officially opened its doors, and the Official Launch Programme Book captured every detail of that historic day. This wasn't just a booklet, it was a symbol of Malaya's financial independence. Following its establishment, the Bank operated from part of the Public Works Department (PWD) Selangor building near Dataran Merdeka (Sultan Abdul Samad Building) before moving to its own headquarters at Jalan Dato Onn, a 9.6 million Malayan dollars project designed by PWD architect Nik Mohamed Nik Mahmood, completed in 1970.

items.title: Why Malaya needed a central bank
items.caption: After the war, 80% of export earnings came from rubber and tin, and the money supply was anchored to sterling and controlled by British banks lending for trade rather than development. The panel's quote from first Finance Minister Tun H.S. Lee: “Malaya needed a central bank.”
items.text: Lahirnya Bank Negara Malaysia / The Birth of Bank Negara Malaysia — 26 Januari 1959. Why Malaya Needed a Central Bank? As Malaya pressed for independence, one truth became clear: a nation must control its money to control its future. After World War II, the economy looked strong on Malaya as the world's largest producer of rubber and tin. But beneath that success lay real risks. About 80% of our export earnings came from just these two commodities, meaning our fortunes rose and fell with global prices we could not control. At the same time, our population was growing rapidly, and the country needed to diversify and industrialise to raise living standards. But this transformation required a financial system capable of supporting new industries, something Malaya did not yet have. Our monetary system was still anchored to the British economy. The Malayan dollar was tied to the pound sterling, and local banking was dominated by British banks focused on financing trade, not domestic development. Recognising the risks, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development recommendation was a detailed study known as the Watson-Caine Report, both emphasising the urgent need for a centralised authority to maintain monetary stability and economic growth. A bold and crucial recommendation was made. “The establishment of the Central Bank in finance and economics since independence, marking a new era of financial responsibility and stability.” — Tun H.S. Lee, First Finance Minister. These ideas laid the foundation for the establishment of Bank Negara Tanah Melayu on 26 January 1959, a key milestone in shaping the nation's economic destiny. In 1963, with the formation of Malaysia, it became Bank Negara Malaysia.
